The Rigid Rotor

What you need to know

  • A diatomic molecule turning with a fixed bond length ReR_eRe​ is the particle on a sphere of Lecture 4.4, with its reduced mass μ\muμ and I=μRe2I = \mu R_e^2I=μRe2​. Its Hamiltonian is L^2/2I\hat{L}^2/2IL^2/2I, so its states are the spherical harmonics YJMJY_J^{M_J}YJMJ​​ and its energies are EJ=ℏ2J(J+1)/2IE_J = \hbar^2J(J+1)/2IEJ​=ℏ2J(J+1)/2I, each (2J+1)(2J+1)(2J+1)-fold degenerate. There is no zero-point rotation.

  • Spectroscopists write the levels in wavenumbers, F(J)=B~J(J+1)F(J) = \tilde{B}J(J+1)F(J)=B~J(J+1), with the rotational constant B~=h/8π2cI\tilde{B} = h/8\pi^2cIB~=h/8π2cI. Light molecules have large B~\tilde{B}B~ (HCl 10.6 cm−1^{-1}−1), heavy ones small (CO 1.9 cm−1^{-1}−1). Either way B~≪kBT\tilde{B} \ll k_BTB~≪kB​T, so many rotational levels are populated at room temperature.

  • A molecule absorbs microwaves only if it has a permanent dipole, and only one rung at a time, ΔJ=±1\Delta J = \pm 1ΔJ=±1: the dipole points along the molecular axis, and the photon carries one unit of angular momentum. The lines fall at 2B~(J+1)2\tilde{B}(J+1)2B~(J+1), evenly spaced by 2B~2\tilde{B}2B~, and the spacing gives the bond length.

  • Line intensities follow the populations (2J+1) e−hcF(J)/kBT(2J+1)\,e^{-hcF(J)/k_BT}(2J+1)e−hcF(J)/kB​T, which rise with the degeneracy and then fall with the Boltzmann factor.

  • In the infrared, rotation rides on vibration. Δv=+1\Delta v = +1Δv=+1 with ΔJ=±1\Delta J = \pm 1ΔJ=±1 gives an R branch above and a P branch below the band origin ν~0\tilde{\nu}_0ν~0​, with a gap where ΔJ=0\Delta J = 0ΔJ=0 would be. Real molecules add two small corrections: B~\tilde{B}B~ shrinks in higher vibrational levels, and fast rotation stretches the bond.

A rotating molecule is a particle on a sphere¶

Lecture 4.4 reduced a rigid dumbbell to one particle of reduced mass μ\muμ on a circle. Let the dumbbell point in any direction and the particle moves on a sphere of radius ReR_eRe​, the bond length. The potential energy does not change as the molecule turns, so all of its energy is the kinetic energy of rotation, L2/2IL^2/2IL2/2I:

H^=L^22I,I=μRe2\hat{H} = \frac{\hat{L}^2}{2I}, \qquad I = \mu R_e^2H^=2IL^2​,I=μRe2​
(1)

Fig. Two atoms a bond length ReR_eRe​ apart, turning about their center of mass (+), move like one particle of reduced mass μ\muμ on a sphere of radius ReR_eRe​.

Lecture 4.4 already found the eigenfunctions of L^2\hat{L}^2L^2, the spherical harmonics, so the problem is solved. For rotating molecules, spectroscopists write JJJ and MJM_JMJ​ in place of lll and mmm:

The rigid rotor
H^ YJMJ=EJ YJMJ,EJ=ℏ22I J(J+1),J=0,1,2,…MJ=−J,…,J\hat{H}\,Y_J^{M_J} = E_J\,Y_J^{M_J}, \qquad E_J = \frac{\hbar^2}{2I}\,J(J+1), \qquad J = 0, 1, 2, \dots \qquad M_J = -J, \dots, JH^YJMJ​​=EJ​YJMJ​​,EJ​=2Iℏ2​J(J+1),J=0,1,2,…MJ​=−J,…,J
(2)

  • Each level is (2J+1)(2J+1)(2J+1)-fold degenerate: the energy does not depend on MJM_JMJ​, the orientation of the rotation in space

  • I=μRe2I = \mu R_e^2I=μRe2​, with μ\muμ the reduced mass and ReR_eRe​ the bond length

  • The gaps grow. EJ+1−EJ=(ℏ2/I)(J+1)E_{J+1} - E_J = (\hbar^2/I)(J + 1)EJ+1​−EJ​=(ℏ2/I)(J+1): two, four, six, ... times ℏ2/2I\hbar^2/2Iℏ2/2I. Each step up in rotation costs more than the last.

  • No zero-point energy. J=0J = 0J=0 has E=0E = 0E=0. Y00Y_0^0Y00​ is the same in every direction: the bond axis points anywhere with equal probability, and nothing rotates. As on the ring of Lecture 4.4, no wall and no potential squeezes the wavefunction. A vibrating bond, by contrast, always keeps 12ℏω\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega21​ℏω (Lecture 4.2).

  • What a state describes. ∣YJMJ(θ,ϕ)∣2\lvert Y_J^{M_J}(\theta, \phi)\rvert^2∣YJMJ​​(θ,ϕ)∣2 is the probability density for the bond axis to point in the direction (θ,ϕ)(\theta, \phi)(θ,ϕ).

Spectroscopists count in wavenumbers¶

As for vibrations in Lecture 4.3, divide each energy by hchchc:

Rotational term values
F(J)=EJhc=B~ J(J+1),B~=h8π2cIF(J) = \frac{E_J}{hc} = \tilde{B}\,J(J+1), \qquad \tilde{B} = \frac{h}{8\pi^2cI}F(J)=hcEJ​​=B~J(J+1),B~=8π2cIh​
(3)

  • B~\tilde{B}B~, the rotational constant, is in cm−1^{-1}−1. A large moment of inertia means a small B~\tilde{B}B~ and closely spaced levels

B~=6.626×10−34 J s8π2 (2.998×1010 cm/s)(2.644×10−47 kg m2)=10.59 cm−1\tilde{B} = \frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}}{8\pi^2\,(2.998\times10^{10}\ \text{cm/s})(2.644\times10^{-47}\ \text{kg m}^2)} = 10.59\ \text{cm}^{-1}B~=8π2(2.998×1010 cm/s)(2.644×10−47 kg m2)6.626×10−34 J s​=10.59 cm−1

Rotation is cheap¶

moleculeB~\tilde{B}B~ (cm−1^{-1}−1)vibration ν~\tilde{\nu}ν~ (cm−1^{-1}−1)kBT/hcB~k_BT/hc\tilde{B}kB​T/hcB~ at 300 K
H2_22​60.941613.4
HCl10.6288620
CO1.932143108
I2_22​0.0372135600

  • Rotational steps are a hundred to ten thousand times smaller than vibrational ones. At room temperature kBT=208k_BT = 208kB​T=208 cm−1^{-1}−1 is far above B~\tilde{B}B~, so many JJJ levels are occupied (below), while nearly every molecule sits in v=0v = 0v=0 (Lecture 4.1).

  • The light hydrides have the largest B~\tilde{B}B~: the moment of inertia depends on the reduced mass, which a hydrogen atom keeps small.

Which transitions light can drive¶

A rotating dipole is an antenna¶

Light pushes on the dipole moment MMM of a molecule (Lecture 4.3). A polar diatomic such as HCl or CO carries a permanent dipole MeM_eMe​: its dipole at the bond length ReR_eRe​, the first term of Lecture 4.3’s M(x)=Me+M′x+…M(x) = M_e + M'x + \dotsM(x)=Me​+M′x+… It points along the molecular axis, and it is about 1.1 D for HCl and 0.11 D for CO. As the molecule turns, the dipole turns with it. Seen along a fixed direction zzz, its component Mz=Mecos⁡θM_z = M_e\cos\thetaMz​=Me​cosθ oscillates at the rotation frequency, so it can exchange energy with light at that frequency.

Source
# synced: rotor_antenna
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyArrowPatch
nf = 40
ts = np.arange(nf) / nf                                     # one loop of the animation = two turns
GREEN, BLUE = "#2f9e44", "#1c7ed6"
T0, T1 = 1.65, 5.25                                         # where the trace starts and ends (time 0 to 1)
tt = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
ring = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
# per row: atom labels, colours, radii, distances of the two atoms from the center of mass, polar?
rows = [(("H", "Cl"), ("white", GREEN), (0.15, 0.27), (0.62, 0.62 / 35), True),
        (("N", "N"), (BLUE, BLUE), (0.22, 0.22), (0.37, 0.37), False)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.2, 5.3))
parts = []
for ax, (labels, cols, rads, (p1, p2), polar) in zip(axes, rows):
    ax.set_xlim(-1.3, T1 + 1.1); ax.set_ylim(-1.32, 1.4); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.plot([0, 0], [-1.22, 1.22], color=GRAY, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)        # the field direction z
    ax.text(0.1, 1.26, "$z$", fontsize=19, color=GRAY, va="center")
    ax.plot([T0, T0], [-1.15, 1.15], color=GRAY, lw=0.9)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(T1 + 0.35, 0), xytext=(T0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=GRAY, lw=0.9,
                                                                     mutation_scale=12, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
    ax.text(T1 + 0.42, -0.1, "$t$", fontsize=19, color=GRAY, va="top")
    ax.text(T0, 1.28, "$M_z$", fontsize=19, ha="center", va="center", color=ORANGE)
    if polar:
        ax.plot(np.cos(ring), np.sin(ring), color=ORANGE, lw=0.9, ls=":", alpha=0.7, zorder=1)  # where the tip runs
        for yv, lab in ((1, "$+M_e$"), (-1, "$-M_e$")):
            ax.plot([T0, T1], [yv, yv], color=GRAY, lw=0.9, ls=":")
            ax.text(T1 + 0.08, yv, lab, fontsize=18, color=GRAY, va="center")
        ax.plot(T0 + (T1 - T0) * tt, np.cos(4 * np.pi * tt), color="#dee2e6", lw=1.8, zorder=1)
    else:
        ax.text(-1.25, -1.1, "$M_e = 0$", fontsize=19, color=ORANGE, va="center")
    (bond,) = ax.plot([], [], color="#adb5bd", lw=6, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=3)
    c1 = Circle((0, 0), rads[0], fc=cols[0], ec="k", lw=1, zorder=4); ax.add_patch(c1)
    c2 = Circle((0, 0), rads[1], fc=cols[1], ec="k", lw=1, zorder=4); ax.add_patch(c2)
    l1 = ax.text(0, 0, labels[0], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, weight="bold", zorder=5,
                 color="k" if cols[0] == "white" else "white")
    l2 = ax.text(0, 0, labels[1], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, weight="bold", zorder=5, color="white")
    arrow = FancyArrowPatch((0, 0), (0, 1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=19, color=ORANGE, lw=3.0,
                            shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, zorder=3.5)                 # over the bond, under the atoms
    if polar:
        ax.add_patch(arrow)
    (arc,) = ax.plot([], [], color="k", lw=1.2, zorder=6)
    th_lab = ax.text(0, 0, r"$\theta$", fontsize=19, ha="center", va="center", zorder=6)
    (link,) = ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=1.1, ls=":", zorder=2)
    (trace,) = ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=2.4, zorder=3)
    (dot,) = ax.plot([], [], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=7, zorder=4)
    parts.append((p1, p2, polar, bond, c1, c2, l1, l2, arrow, arc, th_lab, link, trace, dot))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.99, bottom=0.01, hspace=0.06)

def update(i):
    a = 4 * np.pi * ts[i]                                   # the angle turned so far
    d = np.array([-np.sin(a), np.cos(a)])                   # unit vector along the bond, toward H: the dipole
    th = np.arccos(np.clip(d[1], -1, 1))                    # the polar angle from z, 0 to pi
    side = 1.0 if d[0] <= 0 else -1.0                       # the arc runs from z toward the dipole, the short way
    arcs = np.pi / 2 + side * np.linspace(0, th, 40)
    x_now = T0 + (T1 - T0) * ts[i]
    sel = tt <= ts[i] + 1e-9
    for p1, p2, polar, bond, c1, c2, l1, l2, arrow, arc, th_lab, link, trace, dot in parts:
        P1, P2 = p1 * d, -p2 * d
        bond.set_data([P2[0], P1[0]], [P2[1], P1[1]])
        c1.center, c2.center = (P1[0], P1[1]), (P2[0], P2[1])
        l1.set_position((P1[0], P1[1])); l2.set_position((P2[0], P2[1]))
        if polar:
            arrow.set_positions((0, 0), (d[0], d[1]))
            arc.set_data(0.37 * np.cos(arcs), 0.37 * np.sin(arcs))
            mid = np.pi / 2 + side * th / 2
            th_lab.set_position((0.58 * np.cos(mid), 0.58 * np.sin(mid)))
            th_lab.set_visible(th > np.radians(40))
            link.set_data([d[0], x_now], [d[1], d[1]])
            trace.set_data(T0 + (T1 - T0) * tt[sel], np.cos(4 * np.pi * tt[sel]))
            dot.set_data([x_now], [d[1]])
        else:
            th_lab.set_visible(False)
            trace.set_data(T0 + (T1 - T0) * tt[sel], 0 * tt[sel])
            dot.set_data([x_now], [0])

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=nf, interval=85, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

Fig. HCl (top) and N2_22​ (bottom) turning. HCl’s dipole (orange arrow, pointing from the negative Cl end to the positive H end) turns with the bond. Its height along zzz, Mz=Mecos⁡θM_z = M_e\cos\thetaMz​=Me​cosθ, is traced at the right: it swings between +Me+M_e+Me​ and −Me-M_e−Me​ at the rotation frequency. N2_22​ has no dipole, so its trace stays at zero.

A nonpolar molecule (H2_22​, N2_22​, O2_22​, CO2_22​, CH4_44​) has no permanent dipole, so its rotation is invisible in absorption. (Raman spectroscopy still sees it, through the polarizability.)

One rung at a time: ΔJ=±1\Delta J = \pm 1ΔJ=±1¶

A field along zzz pushes on the zzz component of the dipole, Mecos⁡θM_e\cos\thetaMe​cosθ, where θ\thetaθ is the angle between the bond axis and zzz. The transition dipole of Lecture 4.3 becomes an integral over orientations:

⟨J′MJ′∣M^z∣JMJ⟩=Me∫YJ′MJ′∗ cos⁡θ  YJMJ sin⁡θ dθ dϕ\langle J'M_J'|\hat{M}_z|JM_J\rangle = M_e\int Y_{J'}^{M_J'*}\,\cos\theta\;Y_J^{M_J}\,\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi⟨J′MJ′​∣M^z​∣JMJ​⟩=Me​∫YJ′MJ′​∗​cosθYJMJ​​sinθdθdϕ
(5)

  • From J=0J = 0J=0: cos⁡θ Y00=Y10/3\cos\theta\,Y_0^0 = Y_1^0/\sqrt{3}cosθY00​=Y10​/3​ exactly. The function the field produces is a J=1J = 1J=1 state, so J=1J = 1J=1 is the only level it reaches.

  • In general, cos⁡θ YJMJ\cos\theta\,Y_J^{M_J}cosθYJMJ​​ is a mixture of YJ+1MJY_{J+1}^{M_J}YJ+1MJ​​ and YJ−1MJY_{J-1}^{M_J}YJ−1MJ​​ (a recursion of the spherical harmonics), so JJJ changes by one and MJM_JMJ​ stays. Light polarized in the xyxyxy plane couples through sin⁡θ e±iϕ\sin\theta\,e^{\pm i\phi}sinθe±iϕ and changes MJM_JMJ​ by one as well.

  • Physically, a photon carries one unit ℏ\hbarℏ of angular momentum. Absorbing it changes the molecule’s angular momentum by exactly one unit.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
th = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 801)
dth = th[1] - th[0]
Y0 = np.full_like(th, 1 / np.sqrt(4 * np.pi))
Y1 = np.sqrt(3 / (4 * np.pi)) * np.cos(th)
Y2 = np.sqrt(5 / (16 * np.pi)) * (3 * np.cos(th) ** 2 - 1)
cases = [(r"$J = 0 \to 1$", Y1, 1, "allowed"), (r"$J = 0 \to 2$", Y2, 2, "lobes cancel, forbidden")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.7), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [0.85, 1], "hspace": 0.62, "wspace": 0.12})
for (ax, bx), (title, Yj, n, verdict) in zip(axes.T, cases):
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)
    ax.plot(th, Y0, color=GRAY, lw=1.8, ls="--")
    ax.plot(th, Yj, color=TEAL, lw=2.2)
    ax.plot(th, 0.3 * np.cos(th), color=CARDINAL, lw=2.6)
    for xk, lab, col in ((1.0, r"$Y_0^0$", GRAY), (1.55, r"$\cos\theta$", CARDINAL), (2.15, rf"$Y_{n}^0$", TEAL)):
        ax.text(xk, 0.5, lab, color=col, fontsize=15, ha="center", va="center")
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=16)
    f = 2 * np.pi * Yj * np.cos(th) * Y0 * np.sin(th)       # the phi integral gives 2 pi
    area = np.sum(f) * dth
    bx.fill_between(th, f, 0, where=f > 0, color=PURPLE, alpha=0.45, lw=0)
    bx.fill_between(th, f, 0, where=f < 0, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.55, lw=0)
    bx.plot(th, f, color="k", lw=1.6)
    bx.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)
    bx.set_title(rf"multiply: $Y_{n}^0\,\cos\theta\;Y_0^0\,\sin\theta$", loc="left", fontsize=15)
    bx.set_xlabel(("area = 0" if abs(area) < 1e-3 else f"area = {abs(area):.2f}") + f": {verdict}", fontsize=15,
                  color=PURPLE if abs(area) > 1e-3 else GRAY, weight="bold")
    for a in (ax, bx):
        a.set_xlim(0, np.pi); a.set_yticks([]); a.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
    bx.set_xticks([0, np.pi / 2, np.pi]); bx.set_xticklabels(["0", r"$\pi/2$", r"$\pi$"]); bx.tick_params(labelsize=12)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.62, 0.62); bx.set_ylim(-0.75, 0.75)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.16)
plt.show()

Top: the state Y00Y_0^0Y00​ (gray dashed), the factor cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ from the dipole along the bond axis (red), and a final state (teal), against the angle θ\thetaθ between the axis and the field. Bottom: their product times sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ from the surface element; its area is the transition dipole over MeM_eMe​. It is 1/3=0.581/\sqrt{3} = 0.581/3​=0.58 for J=0→1J = 0 \to 1J=0→1 and zero for J=0→2J = 0 \to 2J=0→2, whose lobes cancel.

Selection rules for rotational absorption
Me≠0,ΔJ=±1,ΔMJ=0,±1M_e \neq 0, \qquad \Delta J = \pm 1, \qquad \Delta M_J = 0, \pm 1Me​=0,ΔJ=±1,ΔMJ​=0,±1
(6)

  • The molecule must have a permanent dipole moment, and JJJ changes by one: absorption from JJJ to J+1J + 1J+1, emission from JJJ to J−1J - 1J−1

Absorption from JJJ to J+1J + 1J+1 takes a photon of wavenumber

Microwave lines of a rigid rotor
ν~J=2B~ (J+1),J=0,1,2,…ν~J+1−ν~J=2B~\tilde{\nu}_J = 2\tilde{B}\,(J+1), \qquad J = 0, 1, 2, \dots \qquad\qquad \tilde{\nu}_{J+1} - \tilde{\nu}_J = 2\tilde{B}ν~J​=2B~(J+1),J=0,1,2,…ν~J+1​−ν~J​=2B~

Example: the bond length of CO

Carbon monoxide absorbs at 3.845, 7.690 and 11.535 cm−1^{-1}−1 (115.27, 230.54 and 345.81 GHz). Find its bond length.

  • The lines are 2B~=3.8452\tilde{B} = 3.8452B~=3.845 cm−1^{-1}−1 apart, so B~=1.9225\tilde{B} = 1.9225B~=1.9225 cm−1^{-1}−1.

  • Moment of inertia:

I=h8π2cB~=6.626×10−34 J s8π2 (2.998×1010 cm/s)(1.9225 cm−1)=1.456×10−46 kg m2I = \frac{h}{8\pi^2c\tilde{B}} = \frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}}{8\pi^2\,(2.998\times10^{10}\ \text{cm/s})(1.9225\ \text{cm}^{-1})} = 1.456\times10^{-46}\ \text{kg m}^2I=8π2cB~h​=8π2(2.998×1010 cm/s)(1.9225 cm−1)6.626×10−34 J s​=1.456×10−46 kg m2
(9)

  • Reduced mass: μ=(12.000)(15.995)27.995\mu = \dfrac{(12.000)(15.995)}{27.995}μ=27.995(12.000)(15.995)​ u =6.856= 6.856=6.856 u =1.1385×10−26= 1.1385\times10^{-26}=1.1385×10−26 kg.

  • Bond length: R=I/μ=1.456×10−46/1.1385×10−26R = \sqrt{I/\mu} = \sqrt{1.456\times10^{-46}/1.1385\times10^{-26}}R=I/μ​=1.456×10−46/1.1385×10−26​ m =1.131×10−10= 1.131\times10^{-10}=1.131×10−10 m =113.1= 113.1=113.1 pm.

Line frequencies are measured to many digits, so microwave spectroscopy gives bond lengths to better than 0.01 pm.

  • Swapping 12^{12}12C for 13^{13}13C leaves the bond length alone but raises μ\muμ, so every line moves (Problem 1). Radio astronomers map the cold gas between the stars through CO’s 115 GHz line.

Line intensities follow the populations¶

How strong a line is depends first on how many molecules start in level JJJ. The Boltzmann factor with the degeneracy 2J+12J + 12J+1 gives:

Populations of rotational levels
NJN0=(2J+1) e−hcB~J(J+1)/kBT\frac{N_J}{N_0} = (2J+1)\,e^{-hc\tilde{B}J(J+1)/k_BT}N0​NJ​​=(2J+1)e−hcB~J(J+1)/kB​T
(10)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
hck, T = 1.438777, 300.0                                   # hc/k_B in cm K
LIGHT = "#cdb9e3"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.6], "wspace": 0.12})
for ax, (name, B, Jn) in zip(axes, (("HCl", 10.44, 16), ("CO", 1.9225, 31))):
    J = np.arange(Jn)
    allJ = np.arange(400)
    q = np.sum((2 * allJ + 1) * np.exp(-hck * B * allJ * (allJ + 1) / T))
    f = (2 * J + 1) * np.exp(-hck * B * J * (J + 1) / T) / q
    top = int(np.argmax(f))
    ax.bar(J, f, width=0.75, color=[PURPLE if j == top else LIGHT for j in J])
    ax.text(top, f[top] + 0.004, rf"$J = {top}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=13, color=PURPLE)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=15, loc="left")
    ax.set_xlabel("$J$", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_ylim(0, f.max() * 1.22); ax.tick_params(labelsize=11.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.8, Jn - 0.2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("fraction of molecules", fontsize=12.5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.08, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.15)
plt.show()

Fig. The fraction of molecules in each rotational level at 300 K, for HCl (B~=10.44\tilde{B} = 10.44B~=10.44 cm−1^{-1}−1) and CO (B~=1.92\tilde{B} = 1.92B~=1.92 cm−1^{-1}−1). The most populated level is darker.

  • The degeneracy 2J+12J + 12J+1 rises and the Boltzmann factor falls, so the populations peak: at J=3J = 3J=3 for HCl and J=7J = 7J=7 for CO at room temperature (Problem 3 finds the peak). The heavier molecule spreads over more levels.

  • Each absorption line inherits the population of its starting level. (For microwave lines the photon energy adds a factor that pushes the strongest line a few JJJ higher.)

print("most populated J:", N.argmax(), "  fraction of molecules there:", round(N.max() / N.sum(), 3))

Rotation rides on vibration: infrared bands¶

An infrared photon changes vvv (Lecture 4.3), but the molecule is also rotating, and a photon must change JJJ by one as well. The energies add (Lecture 4.1):

E~(v,J)=ν~(v+12)+B~ J(J+1)\tilde{E}(v, J) = \tilde{\nu}\left(v + \tfrac{1}{2}\right) + \tilde{B}\,J(J+1)E~(v,J)=ν~(v+21​)+B~J(J+1)
(11)

Starting from (v=0,J)(v = 0, J)(v=0,J), a photon can reach (1,J+1)(1, J + 1)(1,J+1) or (1,J−1)(1, J - 1)(1,J−1):

ΔJ=+1:ν~0+B~(J+1)(J+2)−B~J(J+1)=ν~0+2B~(J+1)ΔJ=−1:ν~0+B~(J−1)J−B~J(J+1)=ν~0−2B~J\begin{aligned} \Delta J = +1:\quad &\tilde{\nu}_0 + \tilde{B}(J+1)(J+2) - \tilde{B}J(J+1) = \tilde{\nu}_0 + 2\tilde{B}(J+1) \\ \Delta J = -1:\quad &\tilde{\nu}_0 + \tilde{B}(J-1)J - \tilde{B}J(J+1) = \tilde{\nu}_0 - 2\tilde{B}J \end{aligned}ΔJ=+1:ΔJ=−1:​ν~0​+B~(J+1)(J+2)−B~J(J+1)=ν~0​+2B~(J+1)ν~0​+B~(J−1)J−B~J(J+1)=ν~0​−2B~J​
(12)
The P and R branches
R branch (ΔJ=+1):ν~R(J)=ν~0+2B~ (J+1),J=0,1,2,…\text{R branch } (\Delta J = +1):\quad \tilde{\nu}_R(J) = \tilde{\nu}_0 + 2\tilde{B}\,(J+1), \qquad J = 0, 1, 2, \dotsR branch (ΔJ=+1):ν~R​(J)=ν~0​+2B~(J+1),J=0,1,2,…
(13)
P branch (ΔJ=−1):ν~P(J)=ν~0−2B~ J,J=1,2,3,…\text{P branch } (\Delta J = -1):\quad \tilde{\nu}_P(J) = \tilde{\nu}_0 - 2\tilde{B}\,J, \qquad J = 1, 2, 3, \dotsP branch (ΔJ=−1):ν~P​(J)=ν~0​−2B~J,J=1,2,3,…
(14)

  • JJJ is the level the molecule starts from, in v=0v = 0v=0; ν~0\tilde{\nu}_0ν~0​ is the band origin, the vibrational wavenumber

  • No line at ν~0\tilde{\nu}_0ν~0​: ΔJ=0\Delta J = 0ΔJ=0 is forbidden for a diatomic

Bottom: the lines they make, lined up under the arrows, for HCl at 300 K. The two branches have lines 2B~2\tilde{B}2B~ apart, with a gap at the band origin ν~0\tilde{\nu}_0ν~0​.

Example: reading the HCl band

The HCl band has its lines nearest the gap at R(0) = 2906.25 and P(1) = 2865.10 cm−1^{-1}−1. Find the band origin and B~\tilde{B}B~, treating HCl as a rigid rotor.

The two lines sit symmetrically about the gap, ν~0±2B~\tilde{\nu}_0 \pm 2\tilde{B}ν~0​±2B~:

ν~0=2906.25+2865.102=2885.68 cm−1,B~=2906.25−2865.104=10.29 cm−1\tilde{\nu}_0 = \frac{2906.25 + 2865.10}{2} = 2885.68\ \text{cm}^{-1}, \qquad \tilde{B} = \frac{2906.25 - 2865.10}{4} = 10.29\ \text{cm}^{-1}ν~0​=22906.25+2865.10​=2885.68 cm−1,B~=42906.25−2865.10​=10.29 cm−1
(15)

The band origin is 2885.98 cm−1^{-1}−1, and the microwave value of B~\tilde{B}B~ is 10.44 cm−1^{-1}−1. The small differences come from the bond being slightly longer in v=1v = 1v=1 (next section).

Try it: pick a molecule and change the temperature. Heat spreads the molecules over higher JJJ, so the branches widen; the “real molecule” setting adds the corrections of the next section.

Beyond the rigid rotor¶

The bond is longer in v=1v = 1v=1¶

A real bond stretches more easily than it compresses (the Morse well of Lecture 4.3), so the average bond length grows with vvv, and B~\tilde{B}B~ shrinks:

B~v=B~e−αe(v+12)\tilde{B}_v = \tilde{B}_e - \alpha_e\left(v + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)B~v​=B~e​−αe​(v+21​)
(16)

For HCl, B~0=10.44\tilde{B}_0 = 10.44B~0​=10.44 and B~1=10.14\tilde{B}_1 = 10.14B~1​=10.14 cm−1^{-1}−1. With B~1\tilde{B}_1B~1​ in the upper level and B~0\tilde{B}_0B~0​ in the lower one, the branches are no longer evenly spaced:

ν~R(J)=ν~0+2B~1+(3B~1−B~0) J+(B~1−B~0) J2\tilde{\nu}_R(J) = \tilde{\nu}_0 + 2\tilde{B}_1 + (3\tilde{B}_1 - \tilde{B}_0)\,J + (\tilde{B}_1 - \tilde{B}_0)\,J^2ν~R​(J)=ν~0​+2B~1​+(3B~1​−B~0​)J+(B~1​−B~0​)J2
(17)
ν~P(J)=ν~0−(B~1+B~0) J+(B~1−B~0) J2\tilde{\nu}_P(J) = \tilde{\nu}_0 - (\tilde{B}_1 + \tilde{B}_0)\,J + (\tilde{B}_1 - \tilde{B}_0)\,J^2ν~P​(J)=ν~0​−(B~1​+B~0​)J+(B~1​−B~0​)J2
(18)

  • Since B~1<B~0\tilde{B}_1 < \tilde{B}_0B~1​<B~0​, the R lines crowd together at high JJJ and the P lines spread apart.

  • Pairs of lines that share an upper or a lower level give B~1\tilde{B}_1B~1​ and B~0\tilde{B}_0B~0​ separately (combination differences).

Fast rotation stretches the bond¶

A rapidly spinning molecule stretches, like a mass on a spring swung in a circle. Its moment of inertia grows and its levels fall slightly below B~J(J+1)\tilde{B}J(J+1)B~J(J+1):

F(J)=B~ J(J+1)−D~ J2(J+1)2,ν~J=2B~ (J+1)−4D~ (J+1)3F(J) = \tilde{B}\,J(J+1) - \tilde{D}\,J^2(J+1)^2, \qquad \tilde{\nu}_J = 2\tilde{B}\,(J+1) - 4\tilde{D}\,(J+1)^3F(J)=B~J(J+1)−D~J2(J+1)2,ν~J​=2B~(J+1)−4D~(J+1)3
(19)

The centrifugal distortion constant D~\tilde{D}D~ is tiny, about 4B~3/ν~24\tilde{B}^3/\tilde{\nu}^24B~3/ν~2: a stiff bond barely stretches (Problem 7).

centrifugal distortionfast rotation stretches the bondrotational level JJJlevels and lines fall slightly at high JJJ

Bigger molecules¶

  • Linear molecules (OCS, HCN, CO2_22​) rotate like diatomics, with one moment of inertia and the same J(J+1)J(J+1)J(J+1) ladder. CO2_22​ has no dipole, so it has no microwave spectrum.

  • Nonlinear molecules turn about three axes (Lecture 4.1), with three moments of inertia. In symmetric tops such as NH3_33​ two of them are equal, and the levels need a second quantum number. Water, with three different moments, has a famously irregular spectrum. These are beyond this course.

Problems¶

Problem 1: Carbon-13¶

The J=0→1J = 0 \to 1J=0→1 line of 12^{12}12C16^{16}16O is at 115.271 GHz. Predict the line of 13^{13}13C16^{16}16O, assuming the same bond length, and compare with the measured 110.201 GHz. Why are such isotope lines useful to astronomers?

Solution

The bond length, and so ReR_eRe​, does not change; only μ\muμ does, and B~∝1/I∝1/μ\tilde{B} \propto 1/I \propto 1/\muB~∝1/I∝1/μ:

μ(12C16O)=(12.000)(15.995)27.995=6.856 u,μ(13C16O)=(13.003)(15.995)28.998=7.172 u\mu(^{12}\text{C}^{16}\text{O}) = \frac{(12.000)(15.995)}{27.995} = 6.856\ \text{u}, \qquad \mu(^{13}\text{C}^{16}\text{O}) = \frac{(13.003)(15.995)}{28.998} = 7.172\ \text{u}μ(12C16O)=27.995(12.000)(15.995)​=6.856 u,μ(13C16O)=28.998(13.003)(15.995)​=7.172 u
(20)
ν(13CO)=115.271 GHz×6.8567.172=110.19 GHz\nu(^{13}\text{CO}) = 115.271\ \text{GHz}\times\frac{6.856}{7.172} = 110.19\ \text{GHz}ν(13CO)=115.271 GHz×7.1726.856​=110.19 GHz
(21)

The measured line is at 110.201 GHz, within 0.01%; the small difference comes from vibrational averaging, which also differs slightly between the isotopes. Each isotopologue has its own lines, so astronomers can count 13^{13}13CO separately from 12^{12}12CO. The main CO line is often so strong that it saturates, while the rarer 13^{13}13CO line still reports how much gas there is.

Problem 2: Which molecules have microwave spectra?¶

Which of these have a pure rotational spectrum: HBr, Cl2_22​, CO2_22​, OCS, H2_22​O, CH4_44​, N2_22​O, CH3_33​Cl? Explain each answer in one line.

Problem 3: The most populated level¶

Treating JJJ as continuous, show that (2J+1) e−hcB~J(J+1)/kBT(2J+1)\,e^{-hc\tilde{B}J(J+1)/k_BT}(2J+1)e−hcB~J(J+1)/kB​T is largest at

Jmax⁡=kBT2hcB~−12J_{\max} = \sqrt{\frac{k_BT}{2hc\tilde{B}}} - \frac{1}{2}Jmax​=2hcB~kB​T​​−21​
(22)

Evaluate it for HCl (B~=10.44\tilde{B} = 10.44B~=10.44 cm−1^{-1}−1) and CO (B~=1.92\tilde{B} = 1.92B~=1.92 cm−1^{-1}−1) at 300 K, and for HCl at 1000 K.

Solution

Write a=hcB~/kBTa = hc\tilde{B}/k_BTa=hcB~/kB​T and differentiate:

ddJ[(2J+1) e−aJ(J+1)]=[2−a (2J+1)2]e−aJ(J+1)=0⟹2J+1=2a\frac{d}{dJ}\left[(2J+1)\,e^{-aJ(J+1)}\right] = \left[2 - a\,(2J+1)^2\right]e^{-aJ(J+1)} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2J + 1 = \sqrt{\frac{2}{a}}dJd​[(2J+1)e−aJ(J+1)]=[2−a(2J+1)2]e−aJ(J+1)=0⟹2J+1=a2​​
(23)

which gives Jmax⁡=kBT/2hcB~−12J_{\max} = \sqrt{k_BT/2hc\tilde{B}} - \frac{1}{2}Jmax​=kB​T/2hcB~​−21​. With kBT/hc=208.5k_BT/hc = 208.5kB​T/hc=208.5 cm−1^{-1}−1 at 300 K:

  • HCl, 300 K: 208.5/20.88−0.5=3.16−0.5=2.7\sqrt{208.5/20.88} - 0.5 = 3.16 - 0.5 = 2.7208.5/20.88​−0.5=3.16−0.5=2.7, so the most populated level is J=3J = 3J=3.

  • CO, 300 K: 208.5/3.84−0.5=7.4−0.5=6.9\sqrt{208.5/3.84} - 0.5 = 7.4 - 0.5 = 6.9208.5/3.84​−0.5=7.4−0.5=6.9, so J=7J = 7J=7.

  • HCl, 1000 K: kBT/hc=695k_BT/hc = 695kB​T/hc=695 cm−1^{-1}−1, 695/20.88−0.5=5.8−0.5=5.3\sqrt{695/20.88} - 0.5 = 5.8 - 0.5 = 5.3695/20.88​−0.5=5.8−0.5=5.3, so J=5J = 5J=5.

Heating or a smaller B~\tilde{B}B~ moves the peak up, but only as a square root.

Problem 4: A thermometer in space¶

In a cold interstellar cloud, CO is at 10 K. Find N1/N0N_1/N_0N1​/N0​ and N2/N0N_2/N_0N2​/N0​. Why can the ratio of the 1→21 \to 21→2 and 0→10 \to 10→1 line strengths serve as a thermometer, and why would a hydride like HCl be a poor one at this temperature?

Problem 5: Deuterium chloride¶

From the HCl constants of Lecture 4.3 (band origin 2886 cm−1^{-1}−1, ν~e=2990\tilde{\nu}_e = 2990ν~e​=2990 and ν~exe=52\tilde{\nu}_ex_e = 52ν~e​xe​=52 cm−1^{-1}−1) and B~e=10.59\tilde{B}_e = 10.59B~e​=10.59 cm−1^{-1}−1, predict B~e\tilde{B}_eB~e​ and the band origin of D35^{35}35Cl. The measured values are 5.45 and 2091 cm−1^{-1}−1.

Solution

Deuterium leaves the bond (its potential) unchanged and only raises the reduced mass:

μ(HCl)=0.9796 u,μ(DCl)=(2.0141)(34.9689)36.9830=1.9044 u,μHClμDCl=0.5144\mu(\text{HCl}) = 0.9796\ \text{u}, \qquad \mu(\text{DCl}) = \frac{(2.0141)(34.9689)}{36.9830} = 1.9044\ \text{u}, \qquad \frac{\mu_{\text{HCl}}}{\mu_{\text{DCl}}} = 0.5144μ(HCl)=0.9796 u,μ(DCl)=36.9830(2.0141)(34.9689)​=1.9044 u,μDCl​μHCl​​=0.5144
(24)

Rotation. B~∝1/μ\tilde{B} \propto 1/\muB~∝1/μ: B~e(DCl)=10.59×0.5144=5.45\tilde{B}_e(\text{DCl}) = 10.59\times0.5144 = 5.45B~e​(DCl)=10.59×0.5144=5.45 cm−1^{-1}−1, as measured.

Vibration, first try. Scaling the band origin by μHCl/μDCl=0.7172\sqrt{\mu_{\text{HCl}}/\mu_{\text{DCl}}} = 0.7172μHCl​/μDCl​​=0.7172 gives 2886×0.7172=20702886\times0.7172 = 20702886×0.7172=2070 cm−1^{-1}−1, 1% low.

Vibration, with anharmonicity. The band origin is ν~e−2ν~exe\tilde{\nu}_e - 2\tilde{\nu}_ex_eν~e​−2ν~e​xe​ (Lecture 4.3), and the two terms scale differently: ν~e∝μ−1/2\tilde{\nu}_e \propto \mu^{-1/2}ν~e​∝μ−1/2 and ν~exe∝μ−1\tilde{\nu}_ex_e \propto \mu^{-1}ν~e​xe​∝μ−1. So

ν~e=2990×0.7172=2144,ν~exe=52×0.5144=26.7,ν~0=2144−2(26.7)=2091 cm−1\tilde{\nu}_e = 2990\times0.7172 = 2144, \qquad \tilde{\nu}_ex_e = 52\times0.5144 = 26.7, \qquad \tilde{\nu}_0 = 2144 - 2(26.7) = 2091\ \text{cm}^{-1}ν~e​=2990×0.7172=2144,ν~e​xe​=52×0.5144=26.7,ν~0​=2144−2(26.7)=2091 cm−1
(25)

in agreement with the measurement. The heavier isotope sits lower in the same well, where the well is more nearly parabolic.

Problem 6: The microwave oven¶

A microwave oven runs at 2.45 GHz. Convert this to cm−1^{-1}−1 and compare with the lowest rotational absorption of water vapor, near 557 GHz. Does the oven drive a rotational transition of water? What do you think heats the food?

Problem 7: Centrifugal distortion in HCl¶

Estimate D~≈4B~3/ν~2\tilde{D} \approx 4\tilde{B}^3/\tilde{\nu}^2D~≈4B~3/ν~2 for HCl (B~=10.59\tilde{B} = 10.59B~=10.59, ν~e=2990\tilde{\nu}_e = 2990ν~e​=2990 cm−1^{-1}−1). How much does it lower the level J=20J = 20J=20, and the line J=20→21J = 20 \to 21J=20→21, compared with the rigid rotor?

Solution
D~≈4 (10.59)3(2990)2=47508.94×106=5.3×10−4 cm−1\tilde{D} \approx \frac{4\,(10.59)^3}{(2990)^2} = \frac{4750}{8.94\times10^{6}} = 5.3\times10^{-4}\ \text{cm}^{-1}D~≈(2990)24(10.59)3​=8.94×1064750​=5.3×10−4 cm−1
(26)

(the measured value is 5.3×10−45.3\times10^{-4}5.3×10−4 cm−1^{-1}−1). For J=20J = 20J=20:

B~J(J+1)=10.59×420=4448 cm−1,D~J2(J+1)2=5.3×10−4×4202=94 cm−1\tilde{B}J(J+1) = 10.59\times420 = 4448\ \text{cm}^{-1}, \qquad \tilde{D}J^2(J+1)^2 = 5.3\times10^{-4}\times420^2 = 94\ \text{cm}^{-1}B~J(J+1)=10.59×420=4448 cm−1,D~J2(J+1)2=5.3×10−4×4202=94 cm−1
(27)

so the level sits 2% below the rigid rotor. The line 20→2120 \to 2120→21 moves by 4D~(J+1)3=4×5.3×10−4×213=19.64\tilde{D}(J+1)^3 = 4\times5.3\times10^{-4}\times21^3 = 19.64D~(J+1)3=4×5.3×10−4×213=19.6 cm−1^{-1}−1, out of 2B~(J+1)=4452\tilde{B}(J+1) = 4452B~(J+1)=445 cm−1^{-1}−1, so it is 4.4% low. The correction grows as J4J^4J4 in the levels and J3J^3J3 in the lines: negligible for the strong low-JJJ lines, important for hot gases.

Problem 8: How fast does a molecule spin?¶

Treat HCl in the level J=10J = 10J=10 classically, with L=J(J+1) ℏL = \sqrt{J(J+1)}\,\hbarL=J(J+1)​ℏ and L=IωL = I\omegaL=Iω. How many turns per second does it make? Compare with its vibrational frequency, 8.65×10138.65\times10^{13}8.65×1013 Hz. Does the bond have time to vibrate during one turn?
